Sanjida

I like answering biological questions with mathematics — population models, length-based estimators, priors and likelihoods. What pulls me next is asking the same questions at the molecular level, where a population's history is written in its DNA. Both point the same way: marine fisheries management built on what the biology actually says.

About

I work on the part of a fishery you can only see in numbers: how much biomass is left, how big fish are when they are first caught, and whether the population being managed is really one population.

My MSc thesis at the Department of Zoology, University of Dhaka, used a year of length–frequency data from two Bay of Bengal landing sites to assess two queenfish stocks with the Length-Based Bayesian Biomass (LBB) method — an approach built for fisheries where age and effort data do not exist. Both stocks came back under pressure, and one of them is being caught far below the size that would maximise its yield.

That result is where my interest turns molecular. A length-based assessment can tell you a stock is shrinking; it cannot tell you how many stocks you were actually looking at. I want to pair assessment work with mitochondrial and genome-wide markers so that management units in the Bay of Bengal are drawn where the biology divides, not where the survey boundaries happen to fall.

Scomberoides commersonnianus

Talang queenfish · n = 722

Slightly overfished
B/BMSY0.95
F/M0.60

Biomass sits just below the level that supports maximum sustainable yield, while fishing mortality is still lower than natural mortality. The stock is slightly overfished but not currently being drawn down further — a position that holds only while pressure stays where it is.

Scomberoides lysan

Doublespotted queenfish · n = 519

Overfished
B/BMSY0.75
F/M2.37

Biomass falls clearly short of the level needed for maximum sustainable yield, and fishing mortality runs at more than twice natural mortality. The stock is overfished and still under heavy pressure, so recovery depends on reducing that pressure.

Questions I want to work on

Three questions that follow from where my assessment work runs out of resolution.

Question 01
Stock assessment → population structure Scomberoides commersonnianus

My LBB assessment put talang queenfish at B/BMSY = 0.95 with a truncated length structure, close to the overfished status Barua et al. (2024) found from 2021 data. But a length-based assessment has to assume one stock, and in this genus that assumption has already failed once — Abdussamad et al. (2022) split a cryptic species, S. pelagicus, off from fish recorded as S. commersonnianus.

The question

Can molecular population genetics reveal hidden population structure in Scomberoides commersonnianus, and does that structure change what a length-based assessment says about management units in the Bay of Bengal?

Question 02
Population structure → conservation Tenualosa ilisha

Hilsa is managed as one national stock across rivers, estuaries and marine waters, but the genetics disagree: NextRAD genotyping found three locally adapted ecotypes (Asaduzzaman et al. 2019), while a 2021 study using cross-species gene enrichment found a single, barely differentiated population. Sanctuary placement and ban timing currently rest on whichever answer is assumed.

The question

How genetically connected are hilsa populations across Bangladesh's rivers, estuaries and marine waters, and can molecular evidence identify biologically meaningful management units for the fishery?

Question 03
Single markers → complete mitogenomes Rastrelliger kanagurta

Most of what is known about Indian mackerel genetics comes from short pieces of mitochondrial DNA — the control region and ATPase genes in Indian waters (Sukumaran et al. 2017), cytochrome b across the Indo-Malay archipelago (Mohammed Akib et al. 2015). A complete mitochondrial genome carries far more variable sites than any single marker, and for the Bay of Bengal no mitogenome data exist for this species at all.

The question

What can complete mitochondrial genomes tell us about the genetic diversity and population differentiation of Indian mackerel in the Bay of Bengal that short mitochondrial markers cannot?

Field & lab

Landing sites, mangrove transects and the bench work in between — where the data actually comes from.

  • SundarbansEcological surveys at Kotka, Dublar Char and Hiron Point — species diversity and habitat condition in the world's largest mangrove forest.
  • Chattogram & Cox's BazarMonthly specimen and environmental data collection at artisanal landing sites, feeding the length–frequency series behind the thesis.
  • Bangabandhu Safari Park, GazipurObservational wildlife survey and habitat monitoring, documenting fauna diversity and park ecosystem dynamics.
  • Water qualityChlorophyll and nutrient analysis on coastal samples.
  • Stock assessmentSpecies identification and classification; LBB and FiSAT II applied to length-frequency series.
  • MolecularPCR amplification and analysis of DNA sequences; training in fish disease diagnosis, marine culture and carp breeding at BFRI, Mymensingh.
